    1                                         I.     Introduction

    2    Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

    3    A.    My name is Ryan M. Lewis, and my business address is 5555 North Grand Boulevard,

    4          Oklahoma City, Oklahoma 73112.

    5    Q.    BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED, WHAT IS YOUR POSITION, AND WHAT

    6          ARE YOUR GENERAL AREAS OF RESPONSIBILITY?

    7    A.    I am employed by C. H. Guernsey and Company (“Guernsey”) in its Analytical Solutions

    8          Group, and my current title is Practice Area Leader for Forecasting and Risk Management.

    9          My primary areas of responsibility include load forecasting, risk management, and power

   10          supply planning.

   11    Q.    PLEASE        BRIEFLY        SUMMARIZE            YOUR        EDUCATIONAL            AND

   12          PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE.

   13    A.    I have a Bachelor of Science degree in Mechanical Engineering. I have been employed by

   14          Guernsey for more than eleven years; please see Exhibit RML-1 for a summary of my

   15          experience.

   17          BEFORE THE OKLAHOMA CORPORATION COMMISSION, ANOTHER

   18          UTILITY COMMISSION, OR IN A UTILITY REGULATORY PROCEEDING

   19          BEFORE        AN    ADMINISTRATIVE           HEARINGS         BODY      IN    ANOTHER

   20          JURISDICTION?

   21    A.    I have not previously provided testimony before the Oklahoma Corporation Commission.

   22          I have, however, provided pre-filed testimony in a utility regulatory proceeding before the

    3    Q.    ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

    4    A.    I am appearing on behalf of the Oklahoma Attorney General (“Attorney General”).

    5    Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING?

    6    A.    The purpose of my testimony is to evaluate Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company’s

    7          (“OG&E” or “Company”) request for approval of its requested Extra Large Power and

    8          Light (“XLPL”) tariff and recommend consumer protections.

    9                                          II.     Summary

   10    Q.    PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY.

   11    A.    In my testimony, I begin by discussing several risks associated with serving new large

   12          load customers, such as stranded investment, cost shifts between classes due to lagging

   13          allocation factors, misallocation of Construction Work in Progress, and upward pressure

   14          on Company rates.

   15           Next, I briefly summarize the Company’s proposed XLPL tariff. I then provide an

   16          overview of each risk I identified at the beginning of my testimony and evaluate the extent

   17          to which the Company’s proposed XLPL tariff addresses each of these concerns.

   18          Afterward, I address the Company’s statement that additional large loads will bring

   19          downward rate pressure for other rate classes. I describe the analysis performed by the

   20          Company that was used to support its conclusion and how it does not appropriately

   21          recognize the costs associated with serving large loads.

   22          Finally, I discuss additional consumer protections that should apply to the Company’s

   23          XLPL customers. I recommend that if future network transmission upgrades are required



                                                        7

    1          to serve XLPL customers, then XLPL customers should pre-fund the portion of those costs

    2          necessary to prevent an increase in transmission-related costs allocated to other customer

    3          classes. I also recommend that the Company update class allocation factors on a more

    4          frequent basis. Additionally, I recommend that the Company develop a mechanism to

    5          ensure the XLPL customers participate in their fair share of any approved returns on

    6          Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”).

    7            III.      Issues Related to Company Serving New Large Load Customers

    8   Q.     WHAT ARE SOME OF YOUR CONCERNS ABOUT THE COMPANY SERVING

    9          NEW LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS AS PROPOSED IN ITS APPLICATION?

   10   A.     There are potential risks to both the Company and its ratepayers from serving new large

   11          load customers. I will discuss four areas of major concern:

   12              •    Risk of stranded investment;

   13              •    Cost shifts between classes due to lagging allocation factors;

   14              •    Misallocation when recovering Construction Work in Progress; and

   15              •    Upward pressure on Company rates (not due to cost shifts).

   16          In my testimony, I discuss each concern by:

   17               •   Explaining how it affects Company ratepayers;

   18               •   Determining if the Company has tried to address the concern with its proposed

   19                   structure of serving large load customers; and

   20               •   Providing my assessment of the Company’s proposed addressal of the risk.

    1    Q.      HAS THE COMPANY PROPOSED A NEW TARIFF TO SERVE LARGE LOAD

    2            CUSTOMERS?

    3    A.      Yes. The Company is requesting approval of a new Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”)

    4            tariff for certain large load customers, as required by Final Order No. 753440 in Case No.

    5            PUD2025-000038. 1

    6    Q.      WHAT WAS THE BASIS FOR THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED XLPL TARIFF?

    7    A.      The proposed XLPL tariff was developed from the framework established through the

    8            Company’s negotiations with Google concerning electric service for three new data center

    9            projects. 2 The Company also considered the requirements of House Bill 2992 and large-

   10            load tariffs and contracts offered by other utilities around the country. 3

   11    Q.      PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED XLPL TARIFF.

   12    A.      The Company stated that the proposed XLPL tariff is intended to establish terms and

   13            conditions for serving new large load customers while protecting other customer classes

   14            from costs associated with the additional investments necessary to serve those customers. 4

   15            To accomplish this, the Company proposes several provisions including the following:

   16                •   Contribution in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”) payments for transmission and

   17                    distribution infrastructure associated with serving new or expanded load; 5

   18                •   Performance security to support the XLPL customer’s financial obligations; 6

   17    A.     No. The Company has correctly recognized the need for special treatment of large load

   18           customers and has addressed some of four areas of major concern that I described.

    1            However, there are several areas of concern not adequately addressed in the Company’s

    2            proposed tariff, which I provide in more detail in the next section of my testimony.

    3                           IV.      Company Addressal of Areas of Concern

    4    Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE CONCERN OF STRANDED INVESTMENT RELATED

    5            TO SERVING LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS.

    6    A.      Stranded investment occurs when infrastructure investments are made to serve loads and

    7            those loads later reduce their contract capacity, relocate, or disconnect from the system

    8            before a utility has fully recovered the costs. Stranded investment is typically associated

    9            with an increase in rates because the costs are still recovered through rates, but the utility

   10            system load has been reduced.

   11    Q.      HOW DOES THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED XLPL TARIFF ADDRESS THE

   12            RISK OF STRANDED INVESTMENT?

   13    A.      The XLPL tariff includes several protections intended to reduce stranded cost risk. These

   14            protections include a requirement to pay 100% Contribution in Aid of Construction

   15            (“CIAC”), 13 an Initial Term period of fifteen years, 14 a monthly minimum charge

   16            regardless of the customer’s demand 15 or energy 16 consumed, a termination exit fee or

   17            capacity reduction fee subject to a 36-month notice 17 (with a requirement to prepay the

    1           Minimum Charges),18 a restriction of Capacity Reduction,19 and required credit support of

    2           five years’ worth of minimum charges.20

    3    Q.     PLEASE EXPLAIN THE RISK OF COST SHIFTS BETWEEN CLASSES DUE TO

    4           LAGGING ALLOCATION FACTORS.

    5    A.     Costs can shift between classes when the allocators used to assign revenue responsibility

    6           do not align with the changes in system load and system cost. If large load customers

    7           rapidly expand their share of system demand, but the demand allocators are not updated to

    8           reflect that shift, the allocation of new capacity costs becomes misaligned with the actual

    9           load on the system. This could cause existing customers to absorb a disproportionately

   10           large share of the costs associated with serving large load customers. In other words, when

   11           allocators are not updated frequently enough, they can fail to reflect the proper cost

   12           causation and, as a result, costs that should be attributed to the large load customers are

   13           shifted onto other rate classes.

   14    Q.     DOES THE PROPOSED XLPL TARIFF ADDRESS THE POTENTIAL FOR COST

   15           SHIFTS BETWEEN CUSTOMER CLASSES DUE TO LAGGING ALLOCATION

   16           FACTORS?

   17    A.     No. Later in the testimony I discuss recommendations on preventing cost shifts resulting

   18           from lagging allocation factors.

    1    Q.    WHAT IS THE RISK OF COST MISALLOCATION WHEN RECOVERING

    2          CONSTRUCTION             WORK         IN        PROGRESS       FOR       LARGE        LOAD

    3          INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENTS?

    4    A.    Potential misallocation of CWIP costs can happen in cases involving the recovery of return

    5          on CWIP for a new resource to serve a new load prior to the load coming online. If the

    6          return on CWIP is recovered prior to the new load coming online, the new load does not

    7          participate in the recovery of the return on CWIP, even though the new load has caused the

    8          need for the new resource and therefore has caused the cost of the return on CWIP. In this

    9          case, customers that did not cause the need for the investment would bear the costs

   10          recovered during the construction period, resulting in a mismatch between cost causation

   11          and cost recovery.

   12    Q.    HOW DOES THE PROPOSED XLPL TARIFF ADDRESS CONCERNS

   13          REGARDING THE RECOVERY OF RETURN ON CONSTRUCTION WORK IN

   14          PROGRESS?

   15    A.    The proposed tariff and accompanying terms and conditions do not directly address this

   16          risk. I will further discuss recovery and allocation of return on CWIP costs later in my

   17          testimony.

   18    Q.    HOW CAN NEW LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS CAUSE UPWARD PRESSURE

   19          ON COMPANY RATES?

   20    A.    Rates typically increase over time as new resources replace retiring old resources. The cost

   21          of new resources is generally higher than the cost of 30-year-old resources that they would

   22          typically replace. Therefore, the utility’s incremental capacity cost is typically higher than

   23          its embedded capacity cost. In effect, the marginal cost of serving the new load becomes a



                                                          13

    1              larger driver of system costs, which can result in upward rate pressure for existing

    2              customers unless appropriate cost allocation mechanisms are in place. When system load

    3              increases rapidly (at a level that exceeds normal load growth patterns), the addition of

    4              newer resources to meet the capacity need can materially increase system rates because

    5              new resources will make up a larger share of the overall resource portfolio.

    6    Q.        HOW DOES THE PROPOSED XLPL TARIFF ADDRESS THE POTENTIAL FOR

    7              UPWARD PRESSURE ON RATES?

    8    A.        The proposed tariff and accompanying terms and conditions do not proactively prevent

    9              upward pressure that may result from the investments necessary to serve new large loads.

   10              However, the XLPL tariff does include a mechanism that could address any adverse rate

   11              impacts to other customer classes. For a more detailed discussion of this mechanism, please

   12              refer to the responsive testimony of Attorney General witness Frank Beling.

   13                                V.       Claim of Downward Rate Pressure

   14    Q.        DOES THE COMPANY INDICATE IN ITS FILING THAT SERVING NEW

   15              LARGE LOADS PROVIDES BENEFITS TO OTHER CUSTOMERS?

   16    A.        Yes. The Company claims that adding large loads will “put downward pressure on rates

   17              for all customer classes, including residential, commercial, and industrial customers.” 21

    1    Q.     HOW DID THE COMPANY QUANTIFY THE POTENTIAL RATE BENEFITS

    2           ASSOCIATED WITH SERVING GOOGLE’S LOAD IN CASE NO. PUD 2026-

    3           00031?

    4    A.     In his Direct testimony in Case No. PUD 2026-000031, Mr. Thenmadathil presented a

    5           modified cost of service study (“COSS”) analysis that concludes consumers would

    6           experience a reduction in rates as a result of providing service to the Google data center

    7           sites. 22 The Company’s analysis (“Modified COSS Analysis”) showed that the proposed

    8           addition of Google data centers to the system would create benefits for an average

    9           residential customer of approximately $1.83/month by 2027, increasing to an estimated

   10           $5.33/month by 2031, and eventually reaching $6.84/month by 2036. 23

   11    Q.     DID THIS MODIFIED COSS ANALYSIS ACCURATELY AND FAIRLY

   12           REPRESENT POTENTIAL RATE IMPACTS?

   13    A.     No, I believe the analysis is misleading. The Company used the most recently approved

   14           cost of service study (“COSS”) from Case No. PUD 2023-000087 as a starting point for

   15           the analysis. 24 The Company modified the existing study to incorporate the load Google

   16           would bring onto the system, using contracted demand and the minimum load factors

   17           indicated in the contract. However, the Company did not include any costs of serving the

   18           new load when conducting this analysis. 25 In the Company’s analysis, the addition of

   19           billing units to the LPL class increases the LPL allocation factors and correspondingly

    1          reduces the allocation factors of the other classes, and therefore, the costs allocated to the

    2          other classes. The costs associated with serving new large loads may be substantial given

    3          the amount of capacity that must be procured to meet requirements.

    4    Q.    PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE FLAW IN THE COMPANY’S MODIFIED COSS

    5          ANALYSIS.

    6    A.    The Company analysis included the new load but no new costs. In effect, the only possible

    7          result of the analysis would be a rate decrease because the analysis added load without

    8          adding any new cost.

    9    Q.    IS IT POSSIBLE FOR AN ELECTRIC UTILITY TO SERVE HUNDREDS OR

   10          EVEN THOUSANDS OF MW OF NEW LOAD WITHOUT INCURRING ANY

   11          COST?

   12    A.    No, this is not currently possible for an electric utility such as the Company. For this reason,

   13          the presentation of the savings analysis by the Company is misleading.

   14                               VI.       Additional XLPL Protections

   15    Q.    DO THE TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF THE XLPL TARIFF PROVIDE

   16          ADEQUATE PROTECTIONS AGAINST SERVING NEW LARGE LOADS?

   17    A.    While the terms and conditions of the XLPL tariff are a step in the right direction and

   18          include several important consumer protections, they do not fully address all of the risks

   19          associated with serving new large load customers. In particular, additional measures are

   20          needed to address the recovery of costs associated with network transmission upgrades,

   21          potential cost shifts resulting from lagging allocation factors, and the recovery and

   22          allocation of Construction Work in Progress.




                                                         16
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 40 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/18/2026 - PAGE 17 OF 22

                                                                 Responsive Testimony of Ryan M. Lewis

    1    Q.    IF FUTURE NETWORK TRANSMISSION UPGRADES ARE IDENTIFIED FOR

    2          A LARGE LOAD CUSTOMER, HOW SHOULD RESPONSIBILITY FOR THOSE

    3          COSTS BE DETERMINED?

    4    A.    For any potential future network transmission upgrades caused by a large load customer,

    5          the large load customer should pre-fund through a CIAC payment the portion of the costs

    6          necessary to prevent an increase in the allocation of overall transmission costs to other

    7          customer classes. In other words, the large load should prefund enough of the network

    8          upgrades such that, when accounting for the changes to Company costs resulting from the

    9          network upgrade (network upgrade costs not pre-funded, network transmission service

   10          charges, changes in allocated SPP transmission costs, etc.) and the new billing units added

   11          to the Company system, the total amount of transmission-related costs allocated to other

   12          customer classes do not increase. This prefunding is independent of the fail-safe

   13          methodology described in the responsive testimony of Attorney General witness Frank

   14          Beling and does not address the same cost impact.

   15    Q.    WHY IS THIS TREATMENT APPROPRIATE?

   16    A.    This treatment is appropriate to align with cost-causation principles. If network upgrades

   17          are required to serve a specific load, that load has caused those necessary upgrades.

   18          Although network upgrades may be characterized as shared system assets that benefit the

   19          broader system, cost-causation principles support assigning the load, at minimum, a portion

   20          of the costs of upgrades needed to serve it.
